pos: n. (the central Italian region of Florence, Siena, Pisa and Lucca, where the evangelical movement of the fifteen-forties took its deepest Italian root and was broken by the Roman Inquisition)
etymology: From Latin Tuscia, the land of the Tusci or Etruscans, the people who held the country before Rome.
biblical_def: Tuscany is the region of central Italy between the Apennines and the Tyrrhenian sea, and for the Reformation it is the most important ground in the peninsula that Rome kept. Its cities had printing, banking, universities and a literate laity, and in the fifteen-thirties and forties the writings of Luther, Melanchthon and Bucer travelled its roads in the packs of merchants. Lucca, Siena and Florence all had circles that read justification by faith and said so; Peter Martyr Vermigli preached at Lucca as prior of San Frediano and carried half his convent out of Italy with him in 1542. In that same year Paul the Third reorganised the Roman Inquisition, and the Tuscan movement had perhaps fifteen years before it was hunted down, recanted or scattered to Geneva, Zurich, Strasbourg and the Grisons. Cosimo the First, made duke in 1537 and grand duke in 1569, cooperated with Rome in return for a crown. The dictionary records Tuscany as the clearest case in Europe of a gospel movement that was not defeated by argument but by a tribunal and a prince, and it declines to call that an argument. What survived went abroad and became the Italian exile churches, so that the word which could not be preached in Florence was preached in London and Geneva by Florentines.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a region as a tract of land of indefinite extent; an exile as one banished from his country; a tribunal as a court of justice; a merchant as one who traffics in goods; and a scatter as a dispersion abroad.
webster_full: REGION, n. A tract of land or space of indefinite extent, usually a tract of some considerable extent; a country; a district.
EXILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country; also, the person banished.
TRIBUNAL, n. The seat of a judge; a court of justice; the bench on which judges sit.
MERCHANT, n. A man who trafficks or carries on trade with foreign countries, or who exports and imports goods.
SCATTER, v.t. To disperse; to dissipate; to separate and drive in different directions.
scriptures: Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
corruption_summary: Central Italian region whose evangelical circles at Lucca, Siena and Florence were broken by the reorganised Roman Inquisition after 1542, scattering their preachers into the exile churches.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the modern habit of reading the failure of the Italian Reformation as a verdict on its doctrine, as though a movement that did not win must have been thin. Tuscany refutes that reading. The men who left were not cranks on the edge of the church: they were priors, canons, physicians and professors, and three of them (Vermigli, Ochino, Zanchi) went straight into chairs of divinity in the Reformed cities. What ended the movement was a tribunal with prisons, a prince who wanted a title, and a frontier guarded against books. Luke describes a scattering of exactly this kind and refuses to read it as defeat: “Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. A gospel movement is not measured by whether it holds a city but by whether the word it carried kept working, and the promise attached to the word does not depend on the magistrate: “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11). The Tuscan exiles taught their own children that the city they had lost was never the city they were promised, which is the sober word Hebrews gives every displaced believer: “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). Paul had already told the churches what to expect of such years, “that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God” (Act 14:22).

“For here have we no continuing city” (Heb 13:14) — the lesson the exiles taught their children.

pos: n. (the Tuscan city of Savonarola, the Medici and the Florentine evangelicals, and the seat of the council of 1439 that attempted union with the Greeks)
etymology: From Latin Florentia, the flourishing town, from florens, blooming.
biblical_def: Florence stands at three points in the history the dictionary keeps. First it is the city of Girolamo Savonarola, prior of San Marco, who from 1490 preached repentance, judgment and the plain sense of Scripture to a city drunk on its own refinement, governed it for four years in all but name, and was hanged and burned in the Piazza della Signoria in 1498 at the instance of Alexander the Sixth. Second it is the seat, from 1439, of the council transferred from Ferrara which declared a union with the Greek church on Roman terms, including papal supremacy and purgatory; the union collapsed when the Greek delegates went home. Third it is a city of evangelical reading in the fifteen-forties, where Bartolomeo Panciatichi and others were examined and recanted, and from which men went to Geneva. The Medici restoration under Cosimo the First closed the question by policy. The dictionary honours Savonarola without making him a Protestant: he never left the Roman doctrine of the mass or of merit, and he died a Dominican. What he had, and what the dictionary records, was a preacher's conviction that the word of God judges a city and that a pulpit is not a decoration.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a city as a large town incorporated with privileges; a preacher as one who discourses publicly on religion; repentance as sorrow for sin with amendment; a council as an assembly for consultation; and union as a joining together.
webster_full: CITY, n. In a general sense, a large town; a corporate town; in Great Britain, a town corporate that has a bishop and a cathedral church.
PREACHER, n. One who discourses publicly on religious subjects; one that inculcates any thing with earnestness.
REPENTANCE, n. Sorrow or deep contrition for sin, as an offense and dishonor to God, with a sincere purpose of amendment.
COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
UNION, n. The act of joining two or more things; concord; agreement and conjunction of mind, will, affections or interest.
scriptures: Mat 5:14
Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked.
Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
corruption_summary: Tuscan city of Savonarola's preaching and death, of the 1439 council of union with the Greeks, and of an evangelical circle broken in the fifteen-forties.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the use of Florence as the standing proof that beauty and learning are their own form of piety. The city that produced the most refined art in Christendom hanged the one man who told it plainly that it was under judgment, and did so with the applause of a pope who was himself a scandal. A culture may be exquisite and unrepentant at the same time, and the Lord's word to a church that had lost its first love is the word Florence needed: “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5). The dictionary does not despise Florentine learning. It denies that learning is a substitute for repentance.

The second paragraph states the principle to recover, which is the public office of preaching. Savonarola's power was not political genius; it was that he read the text and applied it, and the text itself is live: “For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword” (Heb 4:12). Scripture ties a city's standing to the character of its honest men rather than to its revenues, “By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted” (Pro 11:11), and it makes a visible town the figure of a visible church: “A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14). Florence was set on a hill and could not be hid, which is precisely why its pulpit mattered.

pos: n. (the Tuscan republic and see whose university sheltered evangelical readers in the fifteen-forties until the city lost its liberty to Florence in 1555)
etymology: From Latin Saena Julia, the Roman colony on the site, a name of Etruscan origin.
biblical_def: Siena was an independent Tuscan republic for four centuries, a banking city and the seat of a university that drew students from across the Alps. In the fifteen-forties its circles read the evangelical books that came in through Venice and Lucca, and Bernardino Ochino, the Capuchin general whose Lenten sermons had filled Italian cathedrals, was a Sienese; he fled to Geneva in 1542 on the same summons that sent Vermigli north. Aonio Paleario taught rhetoric in the city and was accused of heresy there before he was finally burned at Rome in 1570. The republic's political end came in 1555, when after a siege it was handed over and in 1557 granted to Cosimo of Florence, and the Inquisition followed the new government. The dictionary records Siena as a case where a small free state could not protect a reading public once the great powers settled the religious question over its head. It also records Ochino honestly: he began as the most admired preacher in Italy, served the Italian church at London, and ended his life defending positions on the Trinity and on marriage that the Reformed churches rightly refused. A man may flee Rome and still need correcting.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a republic as a commonwealth without a king; a university as a seminary granting degrees; liberty as freedom from restraint; a siege as the sitting down of an army before a place; and heresy as a fundamental error in religion.
webster_full: REPUBLIC, n. A commonwealth; a state in which the exercise of the sovereign power is lodged in representatives elected by the people.
UNIVERSITY, n. An assemblage of colleges established in any place, with professors for instructing students in the sciences and other branches of learning.
LIBERTY, n. Freedom from restraint; the power of acting as one thinks fit, without any restraint but the laws of nature.
SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
scriptures: Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: Tuscan republic and university city, home of Bernardino Ochino, whose evangelical reading was ended with its liberty when Florence took the state in 1555.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the assumption that leaving a false church settles a man's doctrine. Ochino left Rome under summons and was received with honour, and within twenty years he was publishing on the Trinity and on plurality of wives in terms the Zurich church could not tolerate, and was expelled. The dictionary draws the obvious lesson rather than the fashionable one: the test of a teacher is not what he has repudiated but what he now holds, and the standard is fixed and received, not developing. Jude states it flatly, that believers “should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the duty of oversight. Paul charges elders to watch the flock they did not purchase, “to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28), and he makes the requirement of a minister his grip on the deposit: “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9). The sentence he pronounces on any other message, his own name included in the hypothesis, is the reason the Reformed cities could honour Ochino's courage and still shut their pulpits to him: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8).

pos: n. (the Tuscan maritime city and university whose 1409 council deposed two rival popes and elected a third, and whose 1511 council was called against Julius the Second)
etymology: From Latin Pisae, a name of pre-Roman origin, probably Ligurian or Etruscan.
biblical_def: Pisa was a sea power before Genoa broke it in 1284, and a Florentine possession after 1406, keeping a university that outlasted its independence. Its place in church history is conciliar. In 1409 the cardinals of both obediences, weary of a schism that had run thirty-one years, met at Pisa, declared Gregory the Twelfth and Benedict the Thirteenth deposed for schism and heresy, and elected Alexander the Fifth; neither rival accepted the sentence, so Christendom now had three claimants rather than two, and the knot was not cut until Constance in 1414. In 1511 a second council met at Pisa, summoned by Louis the Twelfth of France and a group of cardinals against Julius the Second, and achieved nothing but a quarrel. The dictionary records Pisa as the plainest demonstration of what conciliarism could and could not do. A council could expose the papacy's claim to be above judgment, since two popes were in fact judged; a council could not supply the thing wanting, which was a standard above the assembly itself. That standard is Scripture, and the Reformation's first premise was not that councils are worthless but that they are not the final court.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a council as a deliberative assembly; a schism as a division in a church; to depose as to divest of office; a claimant as one who demands as his right; and a standard as a rule of measure or judgment.
webster_full: COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice; an ecclesiastical assembly.
SCHISM, n. In a general sense, division or separation; but appropriately, a division or separation in a church or denomination of christians.
DEPOSE, v.t. To lay down; to divest of office; to remove from a throne or other high station.
CLAIMANT, n. A person who claims; one who demands any thing as his right.
STANDARD, n. That which is established by sovereign power as a rule or measure; a test; that by which others are judged.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.
corruption_summary: Tuscan city of the 1409 council that deposed two rival popes and elected a third, demonstrating both the reach and the limits of conciliarism.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the modern claim that the Reformation invented private judgment and that before it the church enjoyed a settled authority. Pisa answers it. A century before Luther the cardinals themselves put two popes on trial, found them schismatic, and deposed them; the papal claim to stand beyond all judgment had already been contradicted by the men who made popes. What the conciliar movement lacked was not nerve but a rule, because an assembly that is itself the highest court can only be corrected by another assembly, and that is the regress Pisa produced. Isaiah names the rule by which any assembly is weighed: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The dictionary is not anti-conciliar; it holds that synods and councils are a real ordinance and may err, which is the historic Reformed position, and that their authority is derived. Paul can therefore charge a church to hold what it has received, “stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle” (2Th 2:15), and in the same breath call the church, not the council, “the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15) — a pillar that holds up the truth rather than manufacturing it. Luke commends the hearers who tested an apostle by the text, “and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11).

pos: n. (the Tuscan hill city and see, birthplace of Guido of Arezzo, the monk whose staff notation made congregational singing teachable)
etymology: From Latin Arretium, an Etruscan town name of uncertain sense.
biblical_def: Arezzo is an ancient Tuscan city east of Siena, an Etruscan and then a Roman town, an independent commune that fell to Florence in 1384. Its largest service to the church was musical. Guido, a Benedictine monk of Arezzo in the eleventh century, set out the lines and spaces of the musical staff and the syllables by which intervals could be learned, so that a singer could read a melody he had never heard instead of memorising it from a master. Before Guido, teaching a congregation or a choir new music took years; after him it took a lesson. Every Reformation psalter in Geneva, Strasbourg, Scotland and England depended on that invention, because a metrical psalm printed with its tune assumes a people who can read notes. The dictionary records this gladly. The Reformation restored congregational singing to the church, and the tool that made the restoration practical was handed down from a Tuscan monk five centuries earlier. Arezzo also gave the church a plain reminder that God's gifts to his people are often prepared long before the generation that needs them, and by men who could not have guessed the use.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a psalm as a sacred song or hymn; to sing as to utter sounds with melody; notation as the act of recording by marks; a congregation as an assembly met for worship; and praise as the commendation of excellence.
webster_full: PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a song composed on a divine subject and in praise of God.
SING, v.i. To utter sounds with various inflections of melodious modulation of voice, as fancy may dictate, or according to the notes of a song or tune.
NOTATION, n. The act or practice of recording any thing by marks, figures or characters.
CONGREGATION, n. A collection or assembly of separate things; an assembly of persons met for the worship of God and for religious instruction.
PRAISE, n. Commendation bestowed on a person for his personal virtues or worthy actions; the expression of gratitude for personal favors conferred.
scriptures: Psa 87:3
Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God. Selah.
Col 1:6
Which is come unto you, as it is in all the world; and bringeth forth fruit, as it doth also in you, since the day ye heard of it, and knew the grace of God in truth:
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
corruption_summary: Tuscan city and see, home of Guido of Arezzo, whose eleventh-century staff notation made the Reformation's congregational psalm-singing teachable.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the people of God are meant to sing, with understanding, out of a book they can read. Guido's staff was a literacy tool, and the Reformers used it as one: the Genevan psalter, the Scottish psalter and the English metrical psalms all assume a household that can be taught a tune at home and bring it to the assembly. Peter states the reason a congregation sings at all, as a body with an office, “that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light” (1Pe 2:9).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is to treat church music as performance by the skilled rather than confession by the whole body. A choir that sings what the congregation cannot is the medieval arrangement returning under a modern name, and the dictionary says so. What Scripture commends is entrance, plainness and understanding: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). The psalmist's own praise is corporate speech about a real place and a real God, “Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God” (Psa 87:3), and Paul measures a gospel's arrival by its fruit in ordinary people, the word “as it is in all the world; and bringeth forth fruit, as it doth also in you” (Col 1:6).

pos: n. (the Tuscan city and see whose 1786 diocesan synod adopted Jansenist and reforming articles and was condemned by Rome in 1794)
etymology: From Latin Pistoria, a town on the road north from Florence, of uncertain sense.
biblical_def: Pistoia is a Tuscan city north-west of Florence, and its name belongs to church history because of a synod. In 1786 Scipione de' Ricci, bishop of Pistoia and Prato, with the support of the grand duke Leopold, gathered a diocesan synod which adopted a programme that looked remarkably like a Catholic reformation from within: the liturgy and the Scriptures in the vernacular, a single altar in each church, preaching restored to the centre, the cult of relics and indulgences curtailed, the authority of the bishop asserted against the Roman curia, and the Augustinian doctrine of grace defended against the Jesuit schools. The articles were substantially Jansenist. Pius the Sixth condemned eighty-five of them in the bull Auctorem fidei in 1794, and Ricci resigned and later submitted. The dictionary records Pistoia as the clearest proof that the questions the Reformation raised did not go away inside the Roman communion: two and a half centuries after Trent a bishop with a duke behind him asked for Scripture in the people's tongue and grace without merit, and Rome answered with a bull. The appeal of the synod was not to novelty but to Augustine and the ancient church.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council; vernacular as native or belonging to one's own country; grace as the free unmerited favour of God; an indulgence as a remission of penalty; and submission as a yielding of one's own will.
webster_full: SYNOD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favor of God; the divine influence which renews the heart and restrains from sin.
INDULGENCE, n. In the Romish church, remission of the punishment due to sins, granted by the pope or church.
SUBMISSION, n. The act of submitting; the act of yielding to power or authority; resignation.
scriptures: Isa 2:3

And many people shall go and say, Come ye, and let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths: for out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Eph 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
corruption_summary: Tuscan see whose 1786 synod under Bishop Ricci adopted vernacular worship, preaching and Augustinian grace, and was condemned by Pius the Sixth in 1794.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the claim that Trent closed the argument and that everything afterwards within the Roman communion was settled contentment. Pistoia disproves it from the inside. A bishop, a prince and a synod asked in 1786 for the Bible in Italian, the service in Italian, one altar, plain preaching and the Augustinian doctrine of grace, and they were condemned by name. The dictionary notes that the appeal was backward rather than forward: Ricci wanted the ancient church, not a new one. Jeremiah describes that posture exactly, and also the answer it usually receives: “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein” (Jer 6:16).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The reforms Pistoia asked for are not Protestant inventions; they follow from the nature of a people who are to be taught. Scripture pictures the nations coming precisely to be instructed, “and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths” (Isa 2:3), and it makes the plainness of the word the mechanism of that teaching: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). The foundation named in the New Testament is apostolic and prophetic writing with Christ as the corner, “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20) — which is why a curia cannot be the floor of the building.

pos: n. (the Umbrian hill city and papal possession, seat of a university and of five papal elections, taken into united Italy in 1860)
etymology: From Latin Perusia, an Etruscan city name of uncertain sense.
biblical_def: Perugia is the chief city of Umbria, set high above the Tiber valley, an Etruscan town, a commune, and from the sixteenth century a possession of the papal state. Five popes were elected in the city during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, when Rome itself was too disorderly to hold a conclave, and its university was founded in 1308. Paul the Third broke the city's resistance to the salt tax in the Salt War of 1540 and built a fortress over the ruins of the noble quarter to hold it; the citizens pulled that fortress down in 1860 when Perugia voted itself into the kingdom of Italy, after papal troops had put down a rising there the year before with considerable bloodshed. The dictionary records Perugia as an example of what happens when a bishop is also a prince with artillery. The temporal power did not make the gospel clearer in Umbria; it made the papacy a landlord, with a landlord's interests, and it taught the people of a Christian city to associate the vicar of Christ with a tax and a garrison. Christ's own account of his servants' weapons is the standing judgment on that arrangement.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines temporal as pertaining to this life; a fortress as a fortified place; a garrison as a body of troops stationed in a fort; dominion as sovereign authority; and a weapon as an instrument of offence.
webster_full: TEMPORAL, a. Pertaining to this life or this world or the body only; secular, as temporal power; opposed to spiritual.
FORTRESS, n. A fortified place; a large and permanent fortification, sometimes including a town.
GARRISON, n. A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town, to defend it against an enemy.
DOMINION, n. Sovereign or supreme authority; the power of governing and controlling.
WEAPON, n. Any instrument of offense; any thing used or designed to be used in destroying or annoying an enemy.
scriptures: (For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them.
Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
corruption_summary: Umbrian hill city and papal possession, held by the fortress Paul the Third built after the Salt War of 1540 and freed by its citizens in 1860.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the temporal power of the papacy, and the dictionary names it as a category error rather than merely a political mistake. A church officer who holds cities must tax, garrison and shoot, and Perugia records all three: a salt tax resisted, a fortress built on a ruined quarter, a rising suppressed. The question is not whether a particular pope governed well but whether the office can hold such power without changing its nature, and Paul's description of the apostolic armoury answers it: “(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)” (2Co 10:4).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the sufficiency of ordinary means. Zechariah's word to a governor rebuilding a temple with no army behind him is the charter of every ministry that cannot command: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). Christ forbade his servants the pattern of civil rule in so many words, “Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them” (Mat 20:25), and he refused the means that would have followed from a kingdom of this sort: “My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36). Perugia's citizens pulled down a fortress that a bishop had built; the dictionary does not pretend that was an attack on religion.

pos: n. (the central Italian region of Assisi, Perugia and Spoleto, long part of the papal state and the cradle of the Franciscan movement)
etymology: From Latin Umbria, the land of the Umbri, an Italic people east of the Tiber.
biblical_def: Umbria is the landlocked region of central Italy east of Tuscany, the only one of the old Italian regions without a coast. Its towns are hill towns: Perugia, Assisi, Spoleto, Gubbio, Todi, Orvieto, Foligno. For most of the Middle Ages and until 1860 the greater part of Umbria belonged to the papal state, and its history is therefore the history of a Christian population governed directly by churchmen. It produced the Franciscan movement at Assisi, the Benedictine house of Norcia where Benedict was born, and a long succession of mystics, hermits and penitential preachers. It produced very little evangelical reading in the sixteenth century, for the plain reason that the Inquisition in the papal state had no competing jurisdiction to work around. The dictionary records Umbria as the test case of papal government over a devout people. The region was not irreligious; it was intensely religious, and it was also poor, heavily taxed and kept from the Scriptures in its own tongue. Devotion without the text is the condition Umbria illustrates, and the dictionary names it as a real spiritual state rather than a sham, and a dangerous one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines devotion as a solemn attention to God in worship; a hermit as one who retires from society; penance as the suffering imposed for sin; zeal as ardour in pursuit of an object; and knowledge as a clear perception of truth.
webster_full: DEVOTION, n. A solemn attention to the Supreme Being in worship; a yielding of the heart and affections to God.
HERMIT, n. A person who retires from society and lives in solitude; a recluse; an anchoret.
PENANCE, n. The suffering, labor or pain to which a person voluntarily subjects himself, or which is imposed on him by authority, as a punishment for his faults.
ZEAL, n. Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; in general, this ardor is a laudable passion.
KNOWLEDGE, n. A clear and certain perception of that which exists, or of truth and fact.
scriptures: Rom 10:2
For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
Hab 2:14
For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
Jas 1:22
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
corruption_summary: Landlocked central Italian region of hill towns, long governed directly by the papacy, intensely devout and kept from the Scriptures in its own tongue.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the sentimental use of Umbria as proof that simple piety is enough and doctrine is for cities. The region was full of devotion, pilgrimage, fasting, and genuine self-denial, and it was kept from the one thing that would have ordered all of it. Paul says exactly this about his own countrymen, with affection and without flattery: “For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2). The dictionary applies the sentence to a Christian region as readily as to an unbelieving one, because the deficiency is the same.

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that knowledge of God is a thing promised to whole populations and not reserved to clerks. The prophet's expectation is saturation, “For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea” (Hab 2:14), and the instrument is a text that reaches the unlearned: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). James then forbids the opposite error, a people who have the text and treat hearing as the whole duty: “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves” (Jas 1:22). Umbria's hill towns wanted the first thing and the dictionary wants both for them.

pos: n. (the Umbrian hill town of Francis and Clare, cradle of the Franciscan movement and of the mendicant orders that followed it)
etymology: From Latin Asisium, an Umbrian town name of uncertain sense.
biblical_def: Assisi is a small Umbrian town on the slope of Monte Subasio, and it is the birthplace of Giovanni Bernardone, called Francis, who in 1206 renounced his father's cloth trade and in 1209 obtained Innocent the Third's approval for a company of preachers living without property. Clare followed with an order of women in 1212. The Franciscans spread across Europe within a generation and became, with the Dominicans, the mendicant arm of the medieval church: mobile, popular, preaching in the open air, and eventually the agents of papal business, including the sale of indulgences that provoked Luther. The dictionary is careful here. Francis's own protest was against wealth, and against a clergy fattened on rents; so far the dictionary agrees with him and says that the protest was needed. What it denies is the theology that grew around him, the stigmata treated as a second passion, the imitation of Christ understood as merit, the poverty made a counsel of perfection for an elite rather than a liberty for all. By 1500 the order Francis founded was a landholder and a seller of pardons, which is the ordinary end of reform that has no doctrine under it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mendicant as a beggar; poverty as destitution of property; a friar as a brother of a religious order; merit as desert of reward; and an order as a regular society of religious persons.
webster_full: MENDICANT, n. A beggar; one who makes it his business to beg alms; one of the begging fraternities in the Romish church.
POVERTY, n. Destitution of property; indigence; want of convenient means of subsistence.
FRIAR, n. An appellation common to the monks of all orders; a brother of a religious order.
MERIT, n. Desert; goodness or excellence which entitles one to honor or reward; worth.
ORDER, n. A regular government or body of persons; a religious fraternity living under a rule.
scriptures: Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Col 2:23
Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
Mat 6:2

Therefore when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may have glory of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
corruption_summary: Umbrian town of Francis and Clare, cradle of the mendicant movement, whose protest against clerical wealth outlived its founder as an order of landholders and pardoners.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the doctrine of merit that attached itself to voluntary poverty, and the dictionary names it without despising the poverty. Francis gave up his property and the church of his day needed the rebuke; what followed was the treatment of that renunciation as a higher way earning a higher reward, and that is precisely the thing Paul excludes from the gospel: salvation is “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9), and the one who is justified is described in terms that leave no room for a ladder, “But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly” (Rom 4:5).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Self-denial is commanded of every believer and is not a special vocation, and Scripture warns that chosen severity can become its own display. Paul says of such rules that they have “a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body” (Col 2:23), and Christ warns against alms that are seen: “They have their reward” (Mat 6:2). The dictionary therefore commends what Francis attacked and refuses what was built on him. A church may need men who hold nothing; it never needs a class of Christians whose poverty purchases what Christ purchased.

pos: n. (the Emilian city and duchy whose evangelical academy was investigated in the fifteen-forties, and the see of the reforming cardinal Giovanni Morone)
etymology: From Latin Mutina, a Roman colony on the Aemilian way, of Etruscan or Ligurian origin.
biblical_def: Modena is a city of the Emilian plain, held by the house of Este as part of the duchy of Ferrara and later a duchy in its own right. In the fifteen-thirties and forties it carried one of the liveliest evangelical circles in Italy, the so-called Modenese academy, where laymen, notaries and physicians read justification by faith and discussed it in the shops and the squares, to the alarm of the authorities. In 1542 the city was required to subscribe a formulary of faith drawn up by Cardinal Gasparo Contarini; many signed and the circle was broken up, though men from it turned up afterwards in Geneva and in the Grisons. The bishop of Modena from 1529 was Giovanni Morone, one of the spirituali, a cardinal, papal legate, and president of the final session of Trent — and himself imprisoned by Paul the Fourth in 1557 on suspicion of heresy, tried, and cleared only after that pope's death. The dictionary records Modena because it shows the Italian situation in miniature: evangelical conviction reaching tradesmen, and a hierarchy in which even a cardinal who hoped for reform could end in the castle of Sant'Angelo.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an academy as a society for promoting learning; a formulary as a prescribed form of profession; a tradesman as one who deals in goods; suspicion as the imagining of guilt without proof; and a legate as an ambassador from the pope.
webster_full: ACADEMY, n. A society of men united for the promotion of arts and sciences in general, or of some particular art.
FORMULARY, n. A book containing stated and prescribed forms, as of oaths, declarations, prayers and the like; a prescribed form.
TRADESMAN, n. A shopkeeper; one who deals in the purchase and sale of goods.
SUSPICION, n. The act of suspecting; the imagination of the existence of guilt, fault or something wrong, without proof.
LEGATE, n. An ambassador; a cardinal or bishop sent as the pope's representative to a sovereign prince.
scriptures: Act 17:6
And when they found them not, they drew Jason and certain brethren unto the rulers of the city, crying, These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also;
For I am with thee, and no man shall set on thee to hurt thee: for I have much people in this city.
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
corruption_summary: Emilian city whose lay evangelical academy was broken by a subscribed formulary in 1542, and see of Cardinal Morone, himself imprisoned on suspicion of heresy.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the management of doctrine by subscription, which is what happened at Modena in 1542 and is a live method still. The circle was not refuted; it was handed a formulary and told to sign, and the men who signed went back to their shops with the question unanswered inside them. A church that governs conviction by signature rather than by teaching produces exactly what Italy produced, outward conformity over a reading public that had already seen something. Luke records what alarmed the magistrates at Thessalonica in words the Modenese authorities would have recognised: “These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also” (Act 17:6).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that the word is not in the magistrate's custody. Paul wrote from prison and said so plainly: “Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). The Lord's promise to a preacher in a dangerous city is a promise about people already given, “for I have much people in this city” (Act 18:10), and the reason Modenese notaries would risk anything for a doctrine is the one Paul gives for his own boldness: the gospel “is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth” (Rom 1:16).
